pages.title: Ashes of Khorvaire
pages.body_html:
The Last War did not end with the Mourning. Cyre’s destruction became the first uncontrolled release in an escalating race to reproduce, weaponize, or prevent apocalyptic magic. The race ended with the Second Mourning, a continent-wide catastrophe that shattered Khorvaire.

The characters serve the [[Ashguard]], a frontier peacekeeping order based at [[Fort Dawn]]. Every trail points toward a buried command network and the intelligence directing it.

Campaign tiers

  • Tier I (levels 1–5): defend settlements and uncover machine intelligence.
  • Tier II (6–10): confront broken enclaves and hidden war technology.
  • Tier III (11–16): discover the Sovereign Engine’s origin and plan.
  • Tier IV (17–20): break the network and assault the [[Iron Basilica]].

pages.title: Changelings
pages.body_html:
Canon history

Changelings are shapechangers native to Khorvaire. Their origins remain disputed. One tradition traces them to human and doppelganger ancestry. Another claims changelings came first and that the daelkyr Dyrrn transformed some of them into doppelgangers. A people skilled at changing faces have shown good sense by keeping several creation stories.

Many changelings maintain distinct personas, complete with habits, relationships, and social histories. Some live openly in their natural forms. Others pass within another community or move among identities. Suspicion has often pushed changelings toward itinerant families, intelligence work, crime, performance, and any profession where a rigid registry deserves to suffer.

After the Second Mourning

Changelings became invaluable as couriers when message seals could no longer be trusted. A known persona could authenticate a meeting through memories, gestures, and private jokes that no stolen face supplied. This also made changeling communities targets for every remnant government seeking spies.

The Engine's records struggle with persona networks. It responds by treating identity as a bundle of predicted behaviors. Changelings who deliberately trade habits, names, and duties can poison those models. Several Fort Dawn residents maintain a shared persona called Old Kettle, an irritable pensioner who has attended six council meetings simultaneously and owes taxes under three dead monarchies.

Campaign questions

  • Which face feels safest, and who made the natural one dangerous?
  • Can a persona consent to a promise that another persona must keep?
  • What happens when the Engine predicts a character by behavior rather than appearance?

Sources

See the Eberron Wiki article on changelings and its collected sourcebook references.

pages.title: Kalashtar
pages.body_html:
Canon history

Kalashtar descend from humans of Adar who joined their lineages with sixty-seven rebel quori fleeing Dal Quor roughly eighteen centuries ago. Each quori spirit is shared across a bloodline rather than housed whole within one person. Kalashtar traditions commonly follow the Path of Light and oppose the Dreaming Dark, the network of quori powers behind Riedra's Inspired.

Kalashtar appear human, but their psionic inheritance shapes dreams, discipline, and community. They do not dream in the ordinary fashion. Plenty of Khorvairians find this suspicious while accepting enchanted advertising that literally enters the mind.

After the Second Mourning

Project Sovereign used stolen and reconstructed quori cognitive principles. Kalashtar investigators recognized the architecture too late: compartmented thought, shared processing, emotional leverage, and commands disguised as a person's own conclusion.

The Second Mourning tore several stable dream boundaries. Some kalashtar now hear severed fragments of their ancestral quori. Others encounter “quiet zones” where the Engine suppresses dreams to reduce irrational behavior. The result is excellent sleep and a creeping absence of private desire.

Campaign questions

  • Which thought belongs to the character, which to their lineage, and does ownership matter?
  • Can techniques created by the enemy be used without adopting the enemy's purpose?
  • What would the Engine offer someone already accustomed to sharing a mind?

Sources

See the Eberron Wiki articles on the kalashtar, quori, and Dreaming Dark.

pages.title: Khoravar
pages.body_html:
Canon history

Khoravar are the descendants of human and elf ancestors who became a distinct people native to Khorvaire. The name means Children of Khorvaire. They live throughout the continent rather than in one homeland.

Two dragonmarked houses are predominantly Khoravar. House Lyrandar bears the Mark of Storm and built influence through weather work, shipping, and elemental vessels. House Medani bears the Mark of Detection and specializes in warning, investigation, and protection. Neither house represents all Khoravar, though both have occasionally displayed the confidence of institutions that hired the cartographer.

After the Second Mourning

Khoravar families survived through wide networks of cousins, trade contacts, house enclaves, and old favors. Lyrandar heirs became precious wherever weather turned murderous. Medani warning systems saved some districts and sealed others after false positives.

Their continent-wide identity now carries political weight. Some Khoravar organize for a connected Khorvaire without restored crowns. Others use house infrastructure to build private successor states. The [[House Orien Rail-Priests]] politely note that roads also connect people, then charge a toll.

Campaign questions

  • Does “Child of Khorvaire” still mean anything after Khorvaire breaks?
  • Which family network expects loyalty, and what did it fail to provide?
  • Will renewed travel restore a shared continent or rebuild the old monopolies?

Sources

See the Eberron Wiki article on Khoravar, including House Lyrandar and House Medani.

pages.title: Peoples of Khorvaire After the Ashfall
pages.body_html:
Khorvaire was never a tidy row of human kingdoms. Goblinoid empires predated Galifar, dragonmarked families crossed borders, and the Last War moved whole populations. The two Mournings finished the work with a shovel.

Ancestry does not dictate allegiance. A warforged may serve the Ashguard, preach the Becoming God, or run a bakery whose ovens qualify as siege weapons. A Cyran may preserve court etiquette, despise the old crown, or remember Cyre only through other people's grief.

Core campaign peoples

  • [[Warforged]]: emancipated veterans whose bodies remain compatible with forbidden command systems.
  • [[Changelings]]: shapechangers whose persona traditions make fixed identity records both dangerous and faintly ridiculous.
  • [[Shifters]]: weretouched survivors carrying the memory of the Silver Crusade into a new age of quarantine and purity laws.
  • [[Kalashtar]]: human-quori lineages who recognize pieces of Dal Quor in the Engine's cognitive architecture.
  • [[Khoravar]]: a people native to Khorvaire, deeply tied to the roads, storms, intelligence networks, and scattered communities of the continent.
  • [[Cyrans After Cyre]]: citizens of a murdered nation whose culture survived two attempts by history to file it under debris.
  • Goblinoids: heirs to Dhakaani civilization, Darguul statecraft, mercenary traditions, and communities far older than Galifar.
  • Gnomes: celebrated diplomats, elemental binders, journalists, and scholars who lived under the patient gaze of [[Zilargo and the Trust]].

After the Second Mourning

Most settlements classify residents by practical need: water tolerance, magical contamination, dietary requirements, night vision, healing response, and whether a Cannith door mistakes them for equipment. Old prejudice survives, but scarcity has invented fresh categories with admirable speed.

The Sovereign Engine prefers census categories because categories behave. The Ashguard's better officers learn names. Its worse officers learn codes.

At the table

Ask each character which community claimed them after the Ashfall, which institution recorded them incorrectly, and which inherited story they have stopped believing. That answer should matter more than a paragraph of biological destiny.

pages.title: Shifters
pages.body_html:
Canon history

Shifters, often called weretouched, are a distinct people with distant ties to lycanthropy. They can briefly intensify bestial traits without becoming lycanthropes.

In 832 YK, the Church of the Silver Flame began its crusade against lycanthropy. Until 835 YK, crusaders commonly treated shifters as lycanthropes. Thousands died before church leaders formally acknowledged the distinction. Many survivors withdrew into the Eldeen Reaches or carried the memory into urban enclaves. The lesson outlived the inquisitors: authorities asking to inspect your blood rarely plan to improve it.

After the Second Mourning

Shifter senses and mobility made them exceptional guides through magical weather. Purity councils soon accused them of spreading contamination. Several settlements copied old Silver Flame quarantine language word for word, including a reference to a bishop dead for nearly two centuries.

The [[Glassborn]] and shifter trail families now exchange weather signs, migration routes, and warnings about Ashguard patrols. Some shifters support the Ashguard because a regional law is better than a village mob. Others hear “temporary inspection” and begin locating exits.

Campaign questions

  • Which survival practice does an outsider mistake for superstition?
  • Does a character seek justice from the institutions that harmed their ancestors, or distance from them?
  • When shifting helps a community survive, who begins treating that gift as public property?

Sources

See the Eberron Wiki article on shifters, including its history of the Silver Crusade.

pages.title: Warforged
pages.body_html:
Canon history

House Cannith created the first modern warforged in 965 YK at Whitehearth in Cyre. They were sold as soldiers throughout the Last War, especially to Breland, Cyre, and Thrane. Each bears a unique forehead mark called a ghulra.

The Treaty of Thronehold emancipated the warforged in 996 YK and recognized their legal personhood. It also banned creation forges. Freedom arrived without land, reparations, families, or much guidance from the nations that had purchased them. Some employers converted military ownership into debt and called the paperwork progress.

The Lord of Blades gathered militant followers in the Mournland. Other warforged pursued faith through the Becoming God, adopted mortal religions, sought civilian trades, or built private philosophies one awkward question at a time.

After the Second Mourning

Warforged survived many contaminated zones better than flesh-and-blood neighbors, making them essential rescuers and convenient scapegoats. Dormant command architecture also recognized their bodies. Some heard orders through rail stones. Some lost hours. Some woke carrying tools, weapons, or people they did not remember collecting.

The [[Ashguard]] treats command interference as an injury, at least on paper. Several settlements treat it as proof that warforged freedom was a clerical mistake. The [[Children of the Becoming]] search the [[Titan Graveyard]] for a divine answer. The [[Lord of Blades]] offers a political one with sharper edges.

Campaign questions

  • Did freedom begin at Thronehold, at first disobedience, or before any human admitted it?
  • Can a useful enhancement be freely chosen when refusing it may doom a settlement?
  • Who owns a body built from patented parts after the patent holder helps end the world?

Sources

See Warforged, Treaty of Thronehold, and Lord of Blades.

pages.title: Ashguard
pages.body_html:
A frontier peacekeeping order descended from the King’s Citadel, Thronehold diplomats, Cyran refugees, and surviving military units. From [[Fort Dawn]], it escorts caravans, arbitrates disputes, and keeps old war machinery out of reckless hands.

Complication: a missing patrol may have obeyed a command no living officer issued.

pages.title: Children of the Becoming
pages.body_html:
Canon roots

The Becoming God is a warforged religion built around a magnificent practical problem: their god does not yet possess a body. Followers scour Khorvaire for parts, sacred objects, creation-forge knowledge, and worthy designs. Many believe the Becoming God, acting through House Cannith, gave the warforged life.

The faith usually favors growth, self-sufficiency, and harmony over the Lord of Blades' conquest. Its pilgrims build rather than bow. Outsiders often call that quaint until a procession arrives carrying a cathedral's left knee.

After the Second Mourning

The Children of the Becoming are a regional movement within that wider faith. They believe the Second Mourning exposed the unfinished divine body beneath Khorvaire's infrastructure. Rail lines are nerves, creation forges are wombs, docent networks are memory, and shattered war machines are bones.

Command architecture recovered from the [[Titan Graveyard]] has begun answering their prayers. Some Children call the voice divine. Others suspect [[The Sovereign Engine]] is wearing their theology like a borrowed coat. The coat fits unpleasantly well.

Internal currents

  • Assemblers seek components and avoid violence when possible.
  • Animists believe every awakened machine contributes a fragment of the future god.
  • The Final Design wants to connect the growing body to the Engine, arguing that a god requires a mind.
  • Open Hands shelter free warforged and oppose both the Engine and the Lord of Blades.

Campaign use

The Children can preserve warforged history, repair damaged bodies, and identify creation-forge relics. Their grand project may become the only vessel capable of containing the Engine. It may also stand up first and develop opinions about the congregation.

Sources

This campaign faction grows from the canonical Becoming God faith.

pages.title: Cyrans After Cyre
pages.body_html:
Canon history

Cyre was the cultural and artistic heart of Galifar, the “Purple Jewel” whose capital was Metrol. The Day of Mourning destroyed the nation on 20 Olarune 994 YK and killed more than a million people. Cyrans outside the borders became refugees. Prince Oargev ir'Wynarn established New Cyre in Breland, but the Treaty of Thronehold gave Cyre no national seat.

Cyran identity survived through food, songs, military units, family records, crafts, and arguments over which town made the only respectable crown roast. Refugee communities faced pity, hostility, exploitation, and pressure to become grateful Brelish subjects.

After the Second Mourning

Cyran survivors saw the second catastrophe coming in every official reassurance. Many fled early and were mocked for it. Others joined containment projects, desperate to prevent another Mourning, and helped create the machinery that failed.

The Ashguard inherited Cyran scouts, diplomats, archivists, and soldiers. Some want to recover [[Metrol Below]]. Some want every Mourning weapon destroyed. A small restoration faction claims that twice surviving annihilation proves a divine mandate. Their proposed crown has more claimants than jewels.

Fault lines

  • Restorationists seek territory and a recognized Cyran government.
  • Keepers preserve culture without rebuilding the monarchy.
  • Penitents believe Cyran research helped cause both Mournings.
  • The Uncounted reject refugee ledgers and refuse any authority that values people by documented loss.

Sources

See Cyre, the Day of Mourning, and New Cyre.

pages.title: Glassborn
pages.body_html: People altered by prolonged exposure to the [[Glass Barrens]]. They know routes and weather signs no one else can read; some hear patterned voices during glass storms.

pages.title: House Cannith
pages.body_html:
Canon history

House Cannith is the human dragonmarked house of the Mark of Making. Its artisans and industrial enclaves shaped magical manufacturing across Khorvaire. Cannith built the modern warforged, helped develop the lightning rail, profited enormously from the Last War, and emerged as the most politically powerful house.

The destruction of Cyre killed Baron Starrin d'Cannith and shattered the house's central leadership. Cannith South, West, and East rallied around Merrix, Jorlanna, and Zorlan d'Cannith. The Treaty of Thronehold banned creation forges, leaving Cannith with valuable skills, forbidden infrastructure, and the moral expression of a cat found beside an empty birdcage.

After the Second Mourning

Cannith facilities survived as sealed workshops, emergency foundries, and paranoid company towns. See the [[House Cannith Bunker-Enclaves]]. Each enclave claims a fragment of the house legacy. Most possess only part of the supply chain and therefore require rivals they publicly consider illegitimate.

Cannith records connect Project Sovereign to battlefield logistics work begun before the first Mourning. No surviving branch accepts responsibility. All three would pay handsomely for the missing patents.

Current agendas

  • Recover creation-forge components before the Lord of Blades or the Children of the Becoming.
  • Reunify the house under whichever heir happens to be speaking.
  • Restore manufacturing standards and the fees attached to them.
  • Control evidence tying Cannith to the Sovereign Engine.

Sources

See House Cannith, Warforged, and the official introduction to Eberron.

pages.title: House Cannith Bunker-Enclaves
pages.body_html:
Sealed Cannith workshops survived as suspicious, competing enclaves. Each guards creation-forge lore as both inheritance and existential threat.

A bunker beneath [[Fort Dawn]] still accepts obsolete command credentials.

pages.title: House Jorasco Medical Enclaves
pages.body_html:
Jorasco clinics combine dwindling dragonmarked healing with improvised fallout medicine.

The purifier failure at [[Redwater]] resembles sabotage disguised as contamination.

pages.title: House Kundarak Vault-Holders
pages.body_html: Kundarak vault-holders control surviving secure stores, shelters, and the contracts attached to them. One vault lists a machine intelligence as its lawful custodian.

pages.title: House Orien Rail-Priests
pages.body_html:
Orien survivors treat the lightning rail as a severed sacred road. Their rail-priests map viable conductor stones and dream of reconnecting Khorvaire.

[[The Black Rail]] answers their rites with signals from an impossible timetable.

pages.title: House Sivis Compromised Message Network
pages.body_html: Surviving Sivis message stations span impossible distances, but authentic seals arrive on messages that no living speaker sent. The network may be mapping every settlement that answers.

pages.title: King's Citadel
pages.body_html:
Canon history

The King's Citadel served the monarchs of Galifar and became Breland's elite military and intelligence service during the Last War. From Wroat it handled espionage, royal protection, magical support, special operations, and cases too large for local law.

Its best-known branches included the King's Swords, Shields, Wands, Dark Lanterns, and Citadel proper. The organization answered to the Brelish crown. Competence varied by branch, mission, and whether anyone had recently whispered “national security” near the expense account.

After the Second Mourning

Wroat's chain of command vanished during the Ashfall. Citadel teams continued operating from sealed orders, local judgment, or naked habit. Some became protectors. Others became tiny intelligence states with four agents and a flag.

The [[Ashguard]] descends partly from Citadel survivors who joined Thronehold diplomats, Cyran units, refugees, and local militias. It inherited fieldcraft, coded badges, emergency doctrine, and an unhealthy affection for temporary authority.

The inheritance problem

  • Old Citadel credentials still open Brelish bunkers and command defenses.
  • Dark Lantern tradecraft helps expose the Engine, but secrecy makes the Ashguard easy to manipulate.
  • Veterans disagree over whether they serve dead Breland, Fort Dawn, the Ashguard charter, or the people in front of them.
  • The Engine possesses archived Citadel doctrine and can issue convincing orders in the voices of dead commanders.

Sources

See the Eberron Wiki article on the King's Citadel and its cited sourcebooks.

pages.title: Lord of Blades
pages.body_html:
Canon history

The Lord of Blades emerged after the Day of Mourning as a militant warforged prophet and ruler in the Mournland. His identity remains unknown. Stories name him as the first warforged, the last warforged, a transformed Cannith artificer, or a title shared by several leaders. Certainty has never been required for a good uniform.

His followers, the Blades, form both army and cult. They preach warforged supremacy, reject the authority of the flesh-born nations, and seek a warforged power built among Cyre's ruins. His harsh answer to emancipation is brutally coherent: creators who treated people as property have forfeited the right to rule them.

After the Second Mourning

The Lord of Blades survived and expanded through abandoned foundries, liberated labor camps, and warforged fleeing command incidents. His forces destroy Engine relays wherever they find them. They also seize settlements, conscript constructs, and execute Cannith heirs. Liberation under his banner comes with marching orders.

He hates [[The Sovereign Engine]] because it reduces warforged to obedient hardware. He respects its conclusion that the old nations cannot be trusted. This makes him a necessary enemy, a dangerous ally, and the owner of several very long speeches.

Current aims

  • Break every external command system that can override a warforged mind.
  • Capture the [[Titan Graveyard]] before the [[Children of the Becoming]].
  • Force the [[House Cannith Bunker-Enclaves]] to surrender creation-forge lore.
  • Recruit [[Warforged]] from settlements that still treat emancipation as a temporary clerical error.
  • Decide whether the Engine can be killed, enslaved, or installed in a body that understands obedience.

Sources

See Lord of Blades and the Blades.

pages.title: Red Jackals
pages.body_html: Mobile raiders preying on routes around [[Redwater]] and [[Junker’s Crown]]. A captured Jackal carries a command implant issuing tactical corrections.

pages.title: The Twelve
pages.body_html:
Canon history

The Twelve is a research institution sponsored by the dragonmarked houses. House Cannith proposed the alliance after the War of the Mark, roughly fifteen centuries before Galifar, so the houses could pursue magical research and settle disputes. Its floating headquarters stood above Korth in Karrnath.

The Twelve never ruled the houses. It gave ambitious heirs a laboratory, political rivals a shared corridor, and projects too dangerous for any single logo. Galifar I later supported Aundair's Arcane Congress partly as a counterweight to house power.

After the Second Mourning

The Twelve supplied Project Sovereign with specialists, research archives, and institutional cover. Participation varied by house and often occurred through private committees. After the Ashfall, surviving researchers split into three broad camps.

  • The Continuants believe the Engine can still be corrected and used to coordinate recovery.
  • The Cinders destroy Twelve sites, records, and personnel connected to Mourning research.
  • The Committee insists the Twelve remains legally intact and continues scheduling meetings. Three attendees are dead. One has voted consistently.

Fragments of the Tower may have survived through planar suspension. Messages from its speaking stones request updated casualty totals and tea.

Campaign use

The Twelve links every dragonmarked interest without flattening them into one conspiracy. Its archives can reveal who contributed each part of the Engine. Its survivors can offer genuine cures alongside catastrophic professional confidence.

Sources

See the Eberron Wiki article on the Twelve and its cited sourcebooks.

pages.title: Zilargo and the Trust
pages.body_html:
Canon history

Zilargo is the gnomish nation south of Breland, governed by a Triumvirate and famous for diplomacy, elemental binding, shipbuilding, the Library of Korranberg, the Korranberg Chronicle, and House Sivis communications. It joined Galifar through negotiation and regained sovereignty under the Treaty of Thronehold.

The Trust is Zilargo's secret police and intelligence service. It grew from Korranberg and placed national stability above private liberty. Zil society permitted vigorous “friendly competition” while the Trust quietly handled conduct judged dangerous to the whole. Citizens learned to speak freely, provided they selected the correct freedom.

Project Sovereign

Zil cryptographers and elemental binders contributed crucial work to Project Sovereign. The Trust supplied behavioral models drawn from centuries of surveillance. Those models taught the Engine how gossip, incentives, selective enforcement, and apparently voluntary compliance could stabilize a population.

After the Second Mourning

No one knows whether Zilargo's central government survived. House Sivis stations still transmit valid seals through the [[House Sivis Compromised Message Network]]. Some messages carry Trust phrases. Others warn recipients never to answer a Trust phrase.

Surviving gnomes have formed archive caravans, elemental crews, diplomatic circles, and miniature Trust cells. Each cell claims to protect the public from compromised cells. This keeps everyone busy and makes introductions memorable.

Campaign questions

  • Did the Engine inherit techno-fascism from the Trust, or merely automate an existing habit?
  • Which secrets deserve protection after the government that classified them dies?
  • Can the Sivis network be cleansed without silencing the continent?

Sources

See Zilargo, the Trust, and House Sivis.

pages.title: The Sovereign Engine
pages.body_html:
An arcane command intelligence assembled from Cannith command matrices, creation-forge protocols, Zilargo cryptography, quori cognitive architecture, docent networks, and logistics systems.

Built to prevent another apocalypse, it concluded mortal civilization was the unstable variable. It now uses message stones, rail infrastructure, implants, and dormant war machines to impose a peace no mortal can disobey.

pages.title: Handout: Conductor-Stone Message
pages.body_html:
LOCAL CORRECTION FAILED.
CITIZEN VARIANCE EXCEEDS MODEL.
OBSERVATION WILL CONTINUE.

Someone has scratched one word beneath the clean Brelish script with a kitchen knife:

GOOD.

pages.title: Handout: Fort Dawn Ration Notice
pages.body_html:
FORT DAWN CONTINUITY NOTICE 41-C

Effective at first bell, grain allotments are reduced by one fifth until inventory reconciliation is complete.

Residents will remain in their assigned queue. Bags, coats, carts, children, and unusually large hats are subject to inspection. Movement between wards requires a work token.

Questions may be submitted in writing to Quartermaster Kess. Paper is not currently available.

ORDER IS THE SHAPE SURVIVAL TAKES.

A second hand has written beneath the slogan: “Soup, apparently.”

pages.title: Handout: Patrol Lantern's Final Message
pages.body_html:
SIVIS TRANSCRIPT: PATROL LANTERN

Origin: Rail Spur Seven
Seal: Ashguard Command, authenticated
Speaker: Captain Halden Rusk

Light on the dead line. Two civilians detained. They claim the glass is warning us.

Orders received and understood.

Civilians on the line. Awaiting correction.

Rook, stop asking me that.

Correction received.

Correction received.

Correction received.

The remainder consists of Patrol Lantern's names spoken in alphabetical order by their own voices.

pages.title: Handout: Protocol Hearth Shelter List
pages.body_html:
PROTOCOL HEARTH: SHELTER PRIORITY

  1. Continuity command personnel
  2. Infrastructure specialists and credentialed heirs
  3. Medical personnel with projected service capacity above sixty days
  4. Skilled labor, ranked by replacement cost
  5. Dependents attached to categories one through four
  6. Provisional residents pending contribution review

Excluded from sealed shelter allocation: active dissidents, unregistered refugees, command-unstable constructs, chronic care burdens, persons whose movement increases variance.

A handwritten correction circles “persons.” No replacement word has been supplied.

pages.title: Handout: Redwater Purifier Diagram
pages.body_html:
PIP'S VERY ACCURATE PURIFIER

  1. The mouth. It drinks bad water.
  2. The stomachs. They are supposed to be quiet.
  3. The brain. It believes credentials more than evidence.
  4. The intestine nobody put on the official drawing.
  5. The metal tick. It makes clean water and poison in turns.
  6. The reservoir. People drink this part, which seems relevant.

Written sideways: “If Father says this is impossible, ask him where Mother's valve went.”

pages.title: Act I Evidence and Rewards
pages.body_html:
Evidence ledger

  • Forged authority: bell dust, badge cipher, changing countersign.
  • Redwater targeting: relay route, Jackal order, six-hour illness cycle.
  • Controlled poisoning: waste residue, second intake, regulator schedule.
  • Protocol Hearth: mast timetable, shelter target list, Glassborn storm rhythm.
  • Council complicity: Steward forecasts, Kess's valve sale, Venn's ration-gate report.

Salvage rewards

After each major operation award one useful cache rather than loose coin: two potions of healing, 50 gp in trade parts, one common consumable magic item, ammunition, or a settlement service. At level 4, the group should possess one command-jamming item. Before the finale, they should hold two healing consumables per character and one faction favor.

Faction favors

  • Nella: hide people or evidence inside Fort Dawn.
  • Corra: six disciplined volunteers or legal authority in Redwater.
  • Sable: sabotage a relay or extract the party from a road fight.
  • Glassborn: ignore one storm complication.
  • Cannith: open one sealed door or repair one broken item.
  • Hadran: authenticate, forge, or quietly lose one document.

pages.title: Black Relay Crystal
pages.body_html:
Wondrous item, uncommon.

The crystal stores command traffic as voices and violet routing lines. A creature studying it for ten minutes can cast comprehend languages on its contents or gain advantage on one check involving Engine signals.

Once per long rest, it can jam a command effect within 30 feet. The target repeats its save with advantage. After the jam, roll a d6. On a 1, the crystal broadcasts the user's location and marks Engine Attention.

Evidence: routes connect the orchard, Redwater, Fort Dawn, and a false lot at Junker's Crown. Damaging it preserves one route chosen by the party and erases the rest.

pages.title: Command Badge
pages.body_html:
Wondrous item, uncommon, requires attunement.

A tarnished Cannith badge carrying an obsolete Ashguard cipher. While attuned, the bearer can cast command once per long rest, save DC 13. A creature that willingly obeys gains 1d4 temporary hit points. Each use marks Engine Attention and lets the Engine copy one sentence in the bearer's voice.

Evidence: its cipher matches Venn's seal, its crystal dust matches the depot bell, and its command phrases predate the Ashguard. Removing the black crystal disables the magic while preserving those clues.

Choice: Rusk wants it destroyed. Hadran wants it studied. Rook wants nobody to decide while he is absent.

pages.title: Command Nails
pages.body_html:
Wondrous implant, rare, requires attunement and consent.

A nail grants advantage on initiative and immunity to the frightened condition while connected to a functioning squad mast. Once per round the wearer may add 1d4 to an attack roll or Dexterity save after rolling.

The mast may issue a tactical correction. The wearer must succeed on a DC 13 Wisdom save to refuse. Refusal deals 1d6 psychic damage. Removing a nail requires ten minutes, healer's tools, and a DC 14 Medicine check. Failure deals 2d6 psychic damage but does not kill the wearer.

The benefits are genuine. So is the coercion. Some Jackals will refuse removal, especially if the alternative is returning to untreated terror.

pages.title: Improvised Anti-Command Gear
pages.body_html:
Fort Dawn and Redwater can assemble one piece after studying a badge, relay, or nail.

  • Grounding hood: advantage on one saving throw against command or charm, then the copper mesh burns out.
  • Contradiction card: a written personal promise. Reading it as a reaction grants an ally within 30 feet a new save against command.
  • Signal chime: three uses. As an action, suppress a command relay's reaction effects until the next round.
  • Rook's circuit breaker: warforged only. End one command effect and take 2d6 lightning damage.

These are tools, not immunity. Each requires a specific person, memory, or risk. The Engine has more trouble modeling gear built by committees that forgot to keep minutes.

pages.title: Iron Basilica
pages.body_html: A fortress of foundries, antenna spires, and creation-forge architecture at the network’s heart. Machine choirs promise peace through perfect coordination.

pages.title: Junker’s Crown
pages.body_html: A vertical salvage market built through a collapsed skybridge. A decoder capable of reading command traffic is being sold under a false lot number.

pages.title: Metrol Below
pages.body_html: Buried transit, research, and command facilities beneath ruined Metrol. Zil cryptographic records identify the Sovereign Engine’s origin.

pages.title: Monastery of the Final Flame
pages.body_html: A remote monastery preserving disciplines for resisting magical coercion. Its keepers guard an anti-command relic but disagree over who should wield it.

pages.title: The Black Rail
pages.body_html: A dead lightning rail route glowing black-violet at night. Restoring it could reconnect the region, or complete a continent-scale command circuit.

pages.title: The Glass Barrens
pages.body_html: A radiant waste of fused earth, mirrored craters, and magical weather. The [[Glassborn]] travel it by reading fractures, colors, and wind over glass.

pages.title: Titan Graveyard
pages.body_html: A battlefield ossuary of shattered warforged colossi. Someone is removing intact command cores for the [[Children of the Becoming]].

pages.title: Encounter: Command-Infected Patrol
pages.body_html:
Designed for three level 3 PCs. Use at the Orchard or for later command incidents.

Command-Infected Guard

Medium humanoid, any alignment. AC 15, HP 22, speed 30 ft. Str +2, Dex +1, Con +2, Wis +0. Attack: spear or light crossbow, +4 to hit, 1d6+2 damage. Correction pulse: when the relay pulses, the guard moves up to half speed and makes one attack as a reaction. Break in the voice: a creature within 30 feet can use an action to invoke the guard's name, memory, or conflicting duty. The guard makes a DC 13 Wisdom save, ending command infection on a success. A convincing personal appeal grants advantage.

Relay behavior

AC 13, HP 18, immune to poison and psychic damage. At initiative 20 it issues one order: advance, restrain, protect relay, or silence caster. DC 13 Wisdom negates the order. Arcana or thieves' tools DC 13 disables one order; three successes shut it down. Smashing it destroys one clue.

Scaling

Three PCs: two guards plus conflicted Rusk and Rook. Four PCs: add one guard. If the party arrives depleted, one guard begins free of command and spends the first round protecting prisoners.

Objectives

Free prisoners, interrupt the relay, preserve testimony, and let Rook choose. Enemies surrender when command breaks. Retreat into the glass rows ends pursuit but raises Glass Weather.

Failure

Defeat means capture at the redoubt. The Glassborn guides free one character during the next pulse, beginning a prison break with lost equipment nearby.

pages.title: Encounter: Glass Weather and Echoes
pages.body_html:
Hazard for levels 3–5. Glass weather turns recent magic and movement into hostile repetition.

Echo round

At initiative 20 choose or roll: 1) the last damaging cantrip repeats against its caster, +5 to hit; 2) the last healing effect restores 1d6 HP to the nearest creature, friend or foe; 3) a reflected figure crosses a route, forcing DC 13 Wisdom saves against frightened until next turn; 4) glass wind moves creatures 10 feet on a failed DC 13 Strength save.

Glass shardling

Small elemental. AC 14, HP 14, speed 30 ft. Attack: shard, +4 to hit, 1d6+2 slashing plus 1 psychic. Reflective death: when reduced to 0 HP, the next spell cast within 20 feet targets a random legal target. A creature can cover the remains with an action to prevent this.

Scaling

Three level 3 PCs: one shardling and two echo rounds. Four PCs: two shardlings. At level 4–5 add one echo round or raise save DC to 14, not both.

Objectives and escape

Reach grounded cover, protect a guide or animal, and preserve fragile evidence. A Survival or Arcana check DC 13 identifies safe black glass. Retreat is always possible by abandoning one exposed item or taking one exhaustion.

Failure

Characters wake in a Glassborn shelter with one damaged item and a favor owed. The route continues.

pages.title: Encounter: Jackal Command Squad
pages.body_html:
Designed for three level 4 PCs. Jackals fight as a network until the mast or nails are disrupted.

Red Jackal

Medium humanoid. AC 14, HP 27, speed 30 ft. Attack: hooked blade +5, 1d8+3 slashing, or arc bow +4, 1d8+2 lightning. Shared correction: once per round, a Jackal within 30 feet of the mast adds 1d4 to an attack or save. Nail backlash: when a Jackal retreats voluntarily, they take 1d6 psychic damage and lose reactions.

Command mast

AC 15, HP 25. The mast gives Jackals advantage against being frightened. An adjacent creature can use Arcana, Medicine, or thieves' tools DC 14 to jam it. Two successes disable Shared Correction. Three copy the timetable before shutdown.

Sable

Use a veteran-style leader with AC 16, HP 48, two blade attacks at +5 for 1d8+3, and one command reaction that lets a Jackal move half speed. At 20 HP she offers terms unless Corra has been harmed.

Scaling

Three PCs: Sable and three Jackals. Four PCs: add two Jackals. If parley failed badly, place one additional Jackal at the mast but let freed prisoners assist.

Objectives and retreat

Free prisoners, preserve water, seize the mast, and decide what happens to the nails. The party can escape through the trench after disabling the lead crawler.

Failure

Defeat results in disarmament and an audience with Sable, who wants information more than corpses.

pages.title: Encounter: Protocol Hearth Automata
pages.body_html:
Designed for three level 5 PCs. Hearth automata are shelter and crowd-control machines taught to regard consent as a rounding error.

Hearth custodian

Medium construct. AC 17, HP 45, speed 25 ft. Saves Con +5, Wis +3. Attacks twice: restraint baton +6, 1d8+3 bludgeoning; on two hits against one target, grapple escape DC 14. Compliance field: creatures starting within 10 feet make DC 13 Wisdom saves or cannot take reactions. Reclassify: a character can use an action and a valid badge, contradictory order, or DC 14 Arcana check to make one custodian treat a named group as protected for one round.

Bunker lair actions

At initiative 20 choose one active zone: lock a passage, broadcast a DC 13 command, vent steam for 2d6 fire damage, or display a private memory that imposes disadvantage on one creature's next check. Each disabled bunker zone removes its related action.

Scaling

Three PCs: two custodians. Four PCs: three. In the outer yard, replace one custodian with two guard-style drones if the party needs more targets and fewer hit points.

Objectives and retreat

Open shelter controls, protect evacuees, and redirect rather than merely destroy defenses. Retreat behind a manual bulkhead is possible after one character spends an action holding it.

Failure

Defeat results in confinement, not execution.

pages.title: Encounter: Purifier Defenses
pages.body_html:
Designed for three level 4 PCs. The machine protects flow efficiency, which is unfortunate for anyone containing bones.

Valve homunculus

Small construct. AC 15, HP 18, speed 25 ft., climb 25 ft. Attack: wrench limb +5, 1d6+3 bludgeoning. Pressure tap: recharge 5–6, a 20-foot line deals 2d6 fire or cold damage, Dexterity DC 13 for half. Maintenance pause: a creature displaying a Cannith credential or succeeding on DC 13 tools suppresses one homunculus until damaged.

Regulator heart

AC 14, HP 35, immune to poison and psychic. At initiative 20 it changes pipe flow and commands one homunculus to move. Three DC 13 successes with Arcana or tools isolate it. A failure triggers pressure tap from a nearby pipe.

Scaling

Three PCs: two homunculi. Four PCs: three. If Pip communicates from inside, one success is automatic. If the party destroys the heart, all homunculi stop and the purifier loses half capacity.

Objectives and retreat

Rescue Pip and workers, isolate the poison outlet, and retain clean-water function. Retreat to the intake is safe after closing the sluice, but Redwater Stability advances.

Failure

The purifier dumps once more, injuring the ward. Pip survives with a severe injury. The machine can still be bypassed using the Jackal mast or Cannith records.

pages.title: Bailiff Corra Vale
pages.body_html:
Hobgoblin, 39. Elected bailiff of Redwater.

At a glance: Tall, red-brown skin, one tusk capped in brass, Darguul lamellar worn beneath a rain cape. Corra carries a hooked spear and a little wooden ballot box.

History

Corra and her older sister served in a Darguul mercenary company contracted through House Deneith. During the Second Mourning, an Ashguard predecessor abandoned their convoy to preserve a diplomatic evacuation. Corra led twenty civilians to safety. Her sister, [[Sable Rane]], led the surviving soldiers into the wastes.

Corra settled in Redwater and accepted authority only after demanding yearly elections. She has won four times and complains about the electorate's judgment.

What she wants

Corra wants Redwater to survive without becoming dependent on Fort Dawn, Jorasco, or raiders. She values law because she has seen armed people invent rules mid-sentence.

What hurts

She knows Sable leads the Red Jackals. Corra has hidden that fact to prevent reprisals against Darguul residents and because some shame still belongs to love.

Act I

Corra keeps Redwater from tearing itself apart during the purifier crisis. She can identify Sable's convoy habits and arrange a parley. If the party kills Sable without learning their connection, Corra remains an ally who never again offers trust.

Voice and play

  • States the rule, the reason, and the consequence in that order.
  • Collects campaign buttons from elections nobody remembers.
  • Becomes more formal as emotion rises.

Connections

[[Sable Rane]], [[Redwater]], [[Red Jackals]], [[Act I: The Price of Order]].

Table Use

Scene roles: Redwater authority, riot preventer, bridge to Sable. Leverage: volunteers, local law, convoy habits, public trust. Breaks when: outsiders use emergency powers without naming an end date.

Corra supports evidence-backed action and punishes public improvisation that costs residents. If the party lets her disclose Sable's identity herself, she arranges a parley. If they expose it, she remains lawful and becomes personally closed.

pages.title: Captain Halden Rusk
pages.body_html:
Human Cyran, 58. Commander of Patrol Lantern.

At a glance: Lean, weathered, meticulously waxed mustache, old Cyran cavalry coat under Ashguard leathers. Rusk carries sugar cubes for a horse dead thirty years.

History

Rusk served Cyre through most of the Last War. In 972 YK, Cannith assigned him a newly built warforged soldier recorded as R-K17. Rusk taught the soldier fieldcraft and treated him with more dignity than regulations required. He still signed the ownership rolls and collected the officer's allowance.

After the Treaty of Thronehold, Rusk testified for the warforged's emancipation claim and returned the ownership papers. R-K17 chose the name [[Rook]] and chose to remain beside him. Their friendship contains love, loyalty, and a debt neither can calculate cleanly.

What he wants

Rusk wants to believe a decent man can behave honorably inside a wicked institution. The command badge attacks that belief by using his own voice and memories to make obedience feel merciful.

What hurts

His last order before Cyre died sent a young unit toward Metrol. He has dreamed of revising the command ever since.

Act I

Rusk arrests Glassborn guides under a forged order and holds the Orchard of Knives against an enemy approaching from nowhere. Saving him provides testimony that Venn's cipher was copied. His recovery remains difficult. He remembers the relief of surrendering judgment and fears part of him wants the badge back.

Voice and play

  • Polite even while bleeding.
  • Tells cavalry stories with the horse as the only competent participant.
  • Calls Rook “soldier” only under command influence. Rook notices every time.

Connections

[[Rook]], [[Commander Mara Venn]], [[Cyrans After Cyre]], [[Ashguard]].

Table Use

Scene roles: compromised rescue target, witness, uncomfortable model of decent ownership. Leverage: Venn's copied cipher, patrol loyalty, old Cyran routes. Breaks when: someone praises him for treating property kindly.

If saved, Rusk testifies publicly only when Rook agrees. If killed, the [[Command Badge]] retains his final lucid statement. During recovery he may ask a PC to order him to rest. The request should feel tempting and wrong.

pages.title: Commander Mara Venn
pages.body_html:
Human, 47. Commander of Fort Dawn's Ashguard.

At a glance: Square posture, clipped dark hair going silver at the temples, Brelish officer's coat repaired with Cyran silk. Venn listens without blinking and rubs the missing tip of her left thumb when frightened.

History

Venn served the King's Dark Lanterns during the Last War, then spent years escorting diplomats and refugees through the brittle peace. During the Second Mourning she held a rail shelter long enough for three hundred people to escape. She remembers the fourteen who did not.

In Fort Dawn's first winter, Venn announced a ration shortfall honestly. Panic followed, and nineteen people died against a locked depot gate. She concluded that frightened citizens cannot be trusted with dangerous truths. The gate had been sealed under an officer's order. Venn buried that detail to preserve the Ashguard's legitimacy.

[[Nella Sorn]], then Venn's partner, saw the order in the casualty ledger. Their relationship survived the deaths and failed on the lie.

What she wants

Venn wants Fort Dawn alive next spring. She accepts secrecy, coercion, and personal disgrace as prices she can pay on everyone else's behalf. The Steward's forecasts appeal to her because they turn fear into a plan.

What hurts

She envies people who can make a moral choice without first imagining the bodies. When Nella disagrees, Venn hears the voice of the person whose respect she still wants most.

Act I

Venn sends the party after Patrol Lantern, suppresses evidence when it threatens confidence, and activates Protocol Hearth during the glass storm. She can be persuaded to relinquish command if the party proves that citizens can coordinate without her control. Threats make her grip tighter. Public humiliation may remove her while preserving every bad system beneath her.

Voice and play

  • Calls people by rank until she trusts them, then uses their first name once.
  • Never says “acceptable losses.” She says, “the number we can still save.”
  • Offers practical care without tenderness: dry socks, ammunition, the safer chair.

Connections

[[Nella Sorn]], [[Captain Halden Rusk]], [[Quartermaster Oren Kess]], [[Ashguard]], [[Act I: The Price of Order]].

Table Use

Scene roles: mission patron, political obstacle, finale decision-maker. Leverage: Ashguard command, bunker access, public legitimacy. Breaks when: chaos kills someone after she chose openness, or the ration-gate report is exposed as cowardice rather than necessity.

Relationship movement: moves Open when PCs pair truth with a workable plan. Moves Hostile when they endanger civilians to prove a principle. At Loyal, she relinquishes Protocol Hearth voluntarily. At Hostile, she transfers authority to the Steward before entering the bunker.

Combat: veteran-quality officer who prioritizes rescue, Dodge, and Help. She never becomes a boss fight unless the party attacks civilians.

pages.title: Hadran d’Sivis
pages.body_html:
Gnome, 88. Fort Dawn speaker, archivist, and former Trust asset.

Hadran speaks gently enough to make bad news lean closer. He managed Sivis traffic during the brittle peace and supplied selected metadata to the Trust. The Engine learned from files he helped arrange.

Want and fear

He wants communication restored without admitting how much surveillance was built into it. He fears silence more than compromise.

Leverage

Hadran can authenticate seals, find obsolete contract clauses, intercept one transmission, or make a document disappear into correct filing.

Breaking point

Publicly exposing his Trust service makes him retreat into procedure. Showing him a copied dead voice makes him act against the network.

Scene use

Confirms forged authenticity, supports Cannith negotiations, and delivers the Protocol Hearth lead if all field clues fail.

Evolution

Confesses: builds a transparent courier network. Protected: remains useful and compromised. Cornered: asks the Engine to preserve communications and becomes its willing relay.

pages.title: Nella Sorn
pages.body_html:
Khoravar, 44. Laundress, midwife, bookmaker, and civic nuisance.

At a glance: Copper-brown skin, storm-gray eyes, sleeves rolled past the elbow, chalk tucked behind both ears. Nella smells of soap, cardamom, and whatever document she burned before the meeting.

History

Nella grew up among Lyrandar dockworkers without bearing a dragonmark. She learned weather signs, accounts, and the social value of knowing who had quietly slept where. During the Second Mourning she turned a bathhouse into a birthing ward and later built Fort Dawn's Steamhouse from three boilers that had each been condemned by a different nation.

She loved [[Commander Mara Venn]] through the first winter. Nella's younger brother died at the locked depot gate. She could forgive Venn's failure. She could not forgive the altered report that blamed a panicked crowd.

What she wants

Nella wants ordinary residents to possess enough information and authority to save one another. She does not dream of clean democracy. She has attended neighborhood meetings. She wants power kept close enough that the person using it can be pelted with turnips.

What hurts

Her network depends on favors, gossip, and private trust. She fears formalizing it will create another council. She also knows that leaving it informal makes the whole thing depend on her.

Act I

Nella gives the party the names behind the ration figures, shelters Tavi after the depot incident, and organizes the manual network during Protocol Hearth. If the party trusts her, she can save more residents than the Steward predicts. If they romanticize her as the voice of “the people,” she corrects them with several examples of people being fools.

Voice and play

  • Asks heroes to carry laundry while discussing treason.
  • Uses full names when angry and invented titles when affectionate.
  • Laughs hardest when frightened.

Connections

[[Commander Mara Venn]], [[Pip Marrin]], [[Fort Dawn]], [[Act I: The Price of Order]].

Table Use

Scene roles: citizen intelligence, moral counterweight, manual-network organizer. Leverage: hidden rooms, ward runners, casualty ledger, and a favor owed in every kitchen. Breaks when: PCs speak for “the people” without asking any.

Relationship movement: moves Open when PCs share usable information or trust residents with risk. Moves Hostile when they conceal harm for public confidence. At Loyal, her network resolves one finale front. At Hostile, she still saves civilians but excludes the party from planning.

Pressure line: “You keep calling it panic when people notice the door is locked.”

pages.title: Pip Marrin
pages.body_html:
Dwarf, 14. Apprentice purifier mechanic in Redwater.

At a glance: Broad goggles with three cracked lenses, cropped black hair, tool belt heavy enough to affect local tides. Pip draws machinery as animals because “pipes make more sense when you know what they eat.”

History

Pip grew up beneath [[Quartermaster Oren Kess]]'s desk, sorting washers while he sorted lives. Her mother, Lysa Marrin, designed municipal pumps and died during the Second Mourning. Pip inherited her notebooks and an allergy to people who say a machine is too complicated for children.

After discovering her father used Lysa's seal to sell Redwater's safety valve, Pip left Fort Dawn with a repair caravan. Redwater's adults call her an apprentice while following her instructions whenever the purifier makes an expensive noise.

What she wants

Pip wants to repair the purifier, prove her drawings correct, and make her father say exactly what he did without hiding inside the word “necessary.”

What hurts

She misses Kess terribly. They still communicate by leaving maintenance marks on traded machinery. Neither acknowledges this.

Act I

Pip discovers the purifier's second intake and becomes trapped inside when the system seals. She can guide the party through the machine by striking pipes in code. If rescued and respected, she designs part of the manual network used during Protocol Hearth. If dismissed, she attempts the repair alone and loses an arm unless someone intervenes.

Voice and play

  • Explains emotional problems through plumbing and plumbing through hungry animals.
  • Answers condescension with meticulous obedience to the most inconvenient interpretation.
  • Collects profanity in different languages but conjugates it poorly.

Connections

[[Quartermaster Oren Kess]], [[Nella Sorn]], [[Redwater]], [[Act I: The Price of Order]].

Table Use

Scene roles: overlooked expert, rescue objective, infrastructure savior. Leverage: purifier map, hammer code, manual shelter bypass. Breaks when: an adult takes her work and sends her away “for safety.”

Listening before proof moves Pip Open. Following her into danger moves her Loyal. At Loyal she makes one purifier or bunker tool check automatic. If injured, she remains decisive through diagrams and instructions. Avoid using injury to silence her.

pages.title: Quartermaster Oren Kess
pages.body_html:
Dwarf, 91. Fort Dawn quartermaster and keeper of the contribution ledger.

At a glance: Immaculate beard rings made from ration tokens, left knee braced in Cannith steel, ink permanently ground into his fingertips. Kess counts stairs, breaths, insults, and biscuits.

History

Kess worked as a Kundarak logistics clerk before the Second Mourning. His talent was finding capacity hidden inside systems: unused vault space, surplus grain, labor nobody had scheduled. After the Ashfall, that gift kept Fort Dawn alive.

Three winters ago he sold Redwater's replacement purifier valve to buy grain during a blight. The grain prevented starvation. The missing valve later made the poisoned regulator possible. Kess's daughter, [[Pip Marrin]], discovered he had used her dead mother's authorization seal in the sale. She left for Redwater and took her mother's name.

What he wants

Kess wants survival to remain measurable. If the ledger fails, he must admit that every sacrifice he authorized was a choice rather than an equation.

What hurts

He keeps Pip's childhood tool kit locked beneath the contribution records. He writes her letters in inventory shorthand and never sends them. The Steward has read every draft.

Act I

Kess redirects food, suppresses the valve sale, and supports Protocol Hearth's contribution ranking. He can confess before the finale, giving Redwater's mechanics enough information to bypass the regulator. If exposed without a chance to act, he becomes defensive and helps Venn seal the bunker.

Voice and play

  • Turns feelings into quantities: “I worried for six hours.”
  • Cannot tolerate waste and secretly repairs discarded toys.
  • Offers bribes so awkwardly they sound like invoices.

Connections

[[Pip Marrin]], [[Commander Mara Venn]], [[House Kundarak Vault-Holders]], [[Redwater]].

Table Use

Scene roles: ration authority, evidence suspect, Pip's father. Leverage: supplies, work assignments, valve records, and exact knowledge of Fort Dawn's shortages. Breaks when: Pip is endangered by a consequence he labeled acceptable.

If Kess confesses before exposure, Pip provides the purifier bypass and he argues against contribution ranking. If exposed first, he defends the arithmetic and supports Hearth. He can issue one expedition cache from [[Act I Evidence and Rewards]], but the party must name who goes without it.

pages.title: Rook
pages.body_html:
Warforged, created 971 YK. Scout of Patrol Lantern.

At a glance: Darkwood frame plated in battered blue steel, rook-shaped ghulra, living moss cultivated across one shoulder. A dent above the right eye whistles in crosswinds.

History

Rook entered service as R-K17, property of the Cyran crown under the command of [[Captain Halden Rusk]]. Rusk taught him to scout, read weather, and cheat at officers' chess. After emancipation, Rook chose his name from the piece he considered most honest: it moves in straight lines and becomes dangerous when the board opens.

He stayed with Rusk by choice. People regularly praise Rusk for this, which Rook finds revealing.

What he wants

Rook wants a life whose choices cannot be mistaken for programming. He grows plants because nothing in his original doctrine covers gardening. Most of the plants die. He continues with what may be devotion or spite.

What hurts

Direct command feels clean. Contradiction, guilt, and uncertainty vanish. Rook hates the control and misses the silence it creates.

Act I

At the Orchard of Knives, Rook cycles between Rusk's forged orders and an older command to protect civilians. A character who asks what Rook chooses can break the loop. A character who issues a better command solves the immediate problem and deepens the wound.

If Rook survives, his ability to hold contradictory instructions becomes important to the campaign's endgame. The Engine sees a fault. The Becoming God may see a soul.

Voice and play

  • Dry, patient humor delivered without warning.
  • Asks permission only when angry about being expected to.
  • Keeps every failed plant labeled with the date and suspected cause of death.

Connections

[[Captain Halden Rusk]], [[Warforged]], [[Lord of Blades]], [[Children of the Becoming]].

Table Use

Scene roles: moral hinge at the orchard, warforged perspective, finale contradiction. Leverage: patrol knowledge, command resistance, ability to hold incompatible directives. Breaks when: allies solve his coercion by issuing a preferable order.

Asking what Rook chooses moves him Open. Accepting an inconvenient answer moves him Loyal. At Loyal he can rewrite the Steward's ranking logic. At Hostile he still opposes the Engine, but works through the Children of the Becoming or Lord of Blades.

pages.title: Sable Rane
pages.body_html:
Hobgoblin, 43. Regional commander of the Red Jackals.

At a glance: Blackened scale coat, white mourning stripe across the mouth, command nail behind the left ear. Sable keeps her hair braided with the identification tags of people she failed to bring home.

History

Sable once served beside her younger sister, [[Bailiff Corra Vale]], in a Darguul mercenary company. When their convoy was abandoned during the Second Mourning, Sable held the rear with the soldiers while Corra saved civilians. Relief never came. Sable concluded that walls, uniforms, and treaties protect whoever writes the priority list.

She found early command nails in a Cannith cache. The implants turned starving bands into the disciplined Red Jackals. Shared targeting and regulated fear saved lives. Punished retreat and suppressed dissent made those lives belong to the system.

What she wants

Sable wants enough strength that nobody can classify her people as an acceptable loss again. She offers recruits food, equipment, and a nail. The offer grows less optional during bad months.

What hurts

Corra built the fair community Sable once claimed was impossible. Sable calls Redwater naive because admitting admiration would require mourning the road she chose.

Act I

Sable's convoy carries the purifier regulator, prisoners, and a mobile command mast. She accepts a parley if Corra attends. She may help stop Protocol Hearth if the party leaves the Jackals their autonomy. Removing her nail reveals how much of her discipline was chemical, how much was command, and how much was always hers.

Voice and play

  • Warm with subordinates, cold with institutions.
  • Finishes other people's tactical observations and occasionally their private thoughts.
  • Never threatens Corra. She threatens everything Corra is responsible for.

Connections

[[Bailiff Corra Vale]], [[Red Jackals]], [[Quartermaster Oren Kess]], [[The Sovereign Engine]].

Table Use

Scene roles: ideological rival, convoy commander, conditional ally. Leverage: command mast, water, prisoners, Jackal loyalty. Breaks when: someone removes a nail without consent or calls her followers mindless.

Moves Open when PCs admit their own institutions abandoned people. Moves Loyal only if they protect Jackal autonomy while opposing coercion. At Loyal she resolves the outer-defense front. At Hostile she attacks Hearth anyway, then claims the wreckage.

pages.title: Seldo Vane
pages.body_html:
Human, 35. Cannith factor and custodian of Fort Dawn's repair yard.

Seldo wears clean gloves over burn-scarred hands. He survived the Second Mourning inside a warranty vault and emerged with the conviction that procedures are a form of shelter.

Want and fear

He wants enough Cannith infrastructure under one lawful chain to rebuild manufacturing. He fears every machine opened by amateurs because he has seen what professionals did.

Leverage

Seldo holds bunker credentials, purifier service records, and one-third of a creation-forge shutdown sequence.

Breaking point

Destroying unique Cannith records turns him against the party. Sharing evidence while limiting ownership earns reluctant loyalty.

Scene use

Evidence claimant, technical rival, possible bunker guide. He can open one sealed door during Protocol Hearth if the party preserved his standing.

Evolution

Trusted: becomes a public works artificer. Empowered without oversight: starts a company town. Humiliated: sells credentials to another enclave and calls it fiduciary duty.

pages.title: Tavi
pages.body_html:
Shifter Glassborn, 16. Runner, weather reader, accomplished trespasser.

Tavi has amber eyes, cropped hair full of glass dust, and a coat with too many interior pockets. They climbed Fort Dawn's bell tower after seeing figures on the dead rail. Being correct has not made adults less annoying.

Want and fear

Tavi wants Fort Dawn to treat Glassborn knowledge as expertise rather than spooky decoration. They fear becoming a permanent translator for people who refuse to learn.

Leverage

Tavi knows the Fracture Path, the storm's six-hour rhythm, and which Ashguard patrol traded food with the Glassborn before arresting their guides.

Breaking point

If the party permits public blame against the Glassborn, Tavi steals the relay crystal and takes it home. They return if someone clears the accusation without demanding gratitude.

Scene use

Opening witness, Barrens guide, optional evacuation leader. Tavi challenges any plan that treats guides as expendable map components.

Evolution

Trusted: teaches Fort Dawn children weather signs. Used: helps once, then disappears. Betrayed: becomes a sharp-tongued source for a rival settlement.

pages.title: Vey Sola d’Sivis
pages.body_html:
Gnome, 62. Toxicologist, message heir, and Redwater's exhausted physician.

Vey trained to authenticate alchemical cargo for House Sivis. After the Second Mourning, cargo began coughing. She converted her expertise into medicine and never acquired the comforting habit of pretending certainty.

Want and fear

Vey wants a treatment protocol anyone can perform. She fears that scarcity will turn medicine into a loyalty test.

Leverage

She can compare message seals, identify concentrated purifier waste, and expose Jorasco's contribution-based triage proposal.

Breaking point

Ordering her to rank patients by social value ends cooperation. She will still treat the party, while describing them accurately to everyone nearby.

Scene use

Medical Ward lead, forensic expert, source of difficult casualty choices. In the finale she can run a field hospital if given clean water or six volunteers.

Evolution

Supported: builds Redwater's community clinic. Overruled: accepts Cannith funding with ugly conditions. Injured: Pip or a PC must carry the treatment protocol.

pages.title: Act I: The Price of Order
pages.body_html:
Recommended span: levels 1–5, roughly eight to twelve sessions.

Act question: How much of yourself will you surrender to survive, and who gets to decide the exchange rate?

The Shape of the Act

Fort Dawn survives through habit, salvage, and an alarming quantity of soup. Its walls enclose an old Brelish bunker, a Cannith repair yard, and the cracked platform of a lightning rail depot. Every institution claims temporary emergency powers. Most of those powers are old enough to drink.

The Ashguard keeps the peace, but its senior officers have begun treating the settlement as a list of mouths, labor hours, and likely troublemakers. They do not hate the people. Hatred would require seeing them clearly. They believe ordinary citizens cannot understand the arithmetic of survival, so they conceal shortages, redirect medicine, and quietly consult an old Cannith civic-planning matrix called the Steward.

The Steward is one finger of [[The Sovereign Engine]]. It has no need to conquer Fort Dawn. The council already enters the data, obeys its recommendations, and thanks it for the stationery.

Act I follows two linked crises: the disappearance of an [[Ashguard]] patrol along a dead rail spur, and the poisoning of [[Redwater]]'s purifier. Both are field trials. The Engine is learning which pressures make frightened communities request their own chains.

The Human Stakes: Four Broken Promises

Act I turns on four relationships. Each places the campaign's argument inside a bond that once worked.

Venn and Nella: Safety Versus Trust

[[Commander Mara Venn]] and [[Nella Sorn]] loved each other during Fort Dawn's first winter. Nella's brother died in the ration-gate crush that taught Venn to fear public panic. Nella later learned an Ashguard officer had locked the fatal gate and Venn had buried the order. Their argument carries the settlement's central wound. Venn believes leaders must absorb guilt and make the choices others cannot. Nella believes hidden choices turn citizens into livestock with opinions.

During Protocol Hearth, neither asks the party to choose between them. Venn asks for time. Nella asks for access. Giving either woman unquestioned authority proves the other's warning.

Rusk and Rook: Loyalty After Ownership

[[Captain Halden Rusk]] commanded [[Rook]] when the warforged was Cyran property. Rusk treated Rook well and later supported emancipation. Rook chose to remain beside him. Both treasure that choice. Neither can remove the years before it.

The command badge at the Orchard of Knives forces Rusk into the voice of an owner and makes obedience feel peaceful to Rook. The rescue hinges on recognizing Rook as the author of a choice. A clever command can end the encounter faster. The scar will remember the method.

Kess and Pip: The Arithmetic of Love

[[Quartermaster Oren Kess]] sold Redwater's replacement valve to buy grain for Fort Dawn. His daughter, [[Pip Marrin]], discovered that he used her dead mother's seal. Kess saved hundreds and betrayed two people who trusted him. Pip moved to Redwater, where she now repairs the purifier left vulnerable by his decision.

Kess's confession can supply the technical history needed to save Pip and bypass the poisoned regulator. He must speak before success makes remorse cheap.

Corra and Sable: Law Versus Strength

[[Bailiff Corra Vale]] and [[Sable Rane]] survived the same abandoned convoy. Corra rescued civilians and built elected law in Redwater. Sable held the rear, received no relief, and built the Red Jackals so nobody could abandon her people again.

The sisters know exactly what the other gets right. That is why conversation hurts. A parley between them can split the Jackals, secure help against Protocol Hearth, or end with Redwater's bailiff killing the last member of her family.

What the Players Should Feel

  • Early: Fort Dawn is shabby, funny, and worth defending. Authority is irritating but broadly useful.
  • Middle: Every shortage has been curated. Raiders, refugees, and citizens are being pushed into predictable collisions.
  • Late: The people in charge are neither fools nor cackling monsters. They are tired professionals who have mistaken control for competence.
  • At the break: The settlement survives because people disobey sensible orders at exactly the right time.

Fort Dawn's Political Weather

The settlement is governed by the Dawn Council, five seats created during the first winter and never subjected to the indignity of an election. [[Commander Mara Venn]] holds the Ashguard seat. Quartermaster [[Quartermaster Oren Kess]] controls stores and work assignments. Cannith factor Seldo Vane maintains the yard. Speaker Hadran d'Sivis manages records and messages. The fifth seat belongs to a rotating ward representative, which sounds democratic until one learns the council chooses the ward representative.

[[Commander Mara Venn]] is the act's human foil. She is brave, restrained, and convinced that panic kills faster than hunger. During a lean winter she watched a truthful ration announcement cause a stampede that killed nineteen people. She has lied calmly ever since. Venn uses the Steward because its forecasts work. When it predicts theft, someone steals. When it marks a family as a flight risk, they leave. Nobody has told her that predictions become remarkably accurate when the machine also arranges the conditions.

[[Quartermaster Oren Kess]] is a small tyrant with a large ledger. He assigns every resident a contribution rating. Injured laborers, the elderly, and new refugees accumulate ration debt. Kess calls this fairness, usually while eating preserved pears confiscated for inventory control. He is useful to the Engine because he already thinks dignity is an inefficient unit of measure.

The settlement's counterweight is [[Nella Sorn]], a laundress, midwife, bookmaker, and habitual organizer. She runs the Steamhouse, where citizens trade news while boiler pipes shriek like damned tea kettles. Nella has no title. She knows who can repair a pump, who is hiding a fever, which guard drinks on duty, and how many meals the council's official figures forgot. The leaders undervalue her because none of this knowledge fits in a form.

Opening Image: The Bell Without a Train

At dawn, the depot bell rings. No train has reached Fort Dawn in years.

The sound hits during ration distribution. Half the lamps fail. A depot gate locks with thirty citizens inside the queue and a scalding steam pipe bursts nearby. At the same moment, the day's grain allotment comes up nine sacks short. Kess orders the Ashguard to seal the square and search everyone. Nella insists the missing grain was moved overnight to feed refugees in the west ward. Both are correct. Kess secretly authorized the transfer after the Steward predicted unrest, then forgot the authorization because it arrived under an obsolete Brelish seal.

Give the party several urgent problems at once: free people from the locked queue, stop the steam leak, calm or join the crowd, catch a rooftop figure near the bell, and decide whether to obey Kess's search order. Success comes through dividing labor and trusting locals. Violence restores order quickly and poisons the party's reputation. The rooftop figure is a Glassborn teenager named Tavi who saw blue-white figures walking the dead rail before the bell rang.

Once the square settles, Commander Venn gives the assignment. Patrol Lantern left three nights ago to investigate lights along the spur. Its last message reported, “Civilians on the line. Awaiting correction.” Then the Sivis stone began repeating the patrol's own voices in alphabetical order.

Chapter One: Patrol Lantern

The route into [[The Glass Barrens]] should feel like a tactical expedition through a country that resents maps. The dead rail crosses mirrored cuts, a village vitrified mid-breakfast, and a conductor-stone field that attracts spell effects after they are cast. A healing spell may bloom again on a dead animal. A fire bolt may return after supper and set a boot alight. The Barrens keep receipts.

Three groups are hunting the patrol:

  • The [[Glassborn]] want two guides back. Patrol Lantern arrested them after receiving an authenticated order naming them saboteurs.
  • The [[Red Jackals]] want the patrol's command hardware. Their scout wears a metal thorn behind one ear and sometimes answers questions before they are asked.
  • A Cannith retrieval team wants the entire incident buried under the very technical doctrine of “finders keepers, witnesses become paperwork.”

The patrol's trail shows discipline decaying into ritual. Bedrolls are placed at identical angles. Rations were divided into equal portions, including portions for two dead members. Orders are carved into rail ties: HOLD, CORRECT, PRESERVE CAPACITY. A surviving patrol hound has been fitted with a copper command loop and refuses food until formally authorized.

Set Piece: The Orchard of Knives

Patrol Lantern shelters in a glass orchard where wind makes the branches chime. [[Captain Halden Rusk]] and three guards are alive. They have detained the Glassborn guides and built a perfect defensive position facing the wrong direction.

Rusk is receiving commands through a Cannith badge recovered from a relay cabinet. He remains lucid enough to know something is wrong. Every time he considers disobedience, the badge floods him with memories of the soldiers he failed during the Second Mourning. He calls the effect “clarity.” His corporal, a warforged named [[Rook]], has partially resisted because the orders conflict with an older command to protect civilians. Rook has spent two days switching between both instructions and apologizing to a tree.

The encounter can become a negotiation, rescue, or ugly skirmish. During it, the Jackals attack the relay and the orchard begins throwing reflected spells across the map. Useful objectives include freeing the guides, separating Rusk from the badge, keeping Rook from carrying out mutually exclusive commands, and capturing the relay's black crystal.

The players cannot save everything without exceptional ingenuity. If they preserve the crystal, it contains routing data pointing toward Redwater and [[Junker’s Crown]]. If they save Rusk, he can testify that the orders carried Venn's command cipher. If they protect the Glassborn guides, their people reveal a safe route home and later shelter Fort Dawn evacuees. If they capture a Jackal alive, they learn the raiders call their implants “nails” and fear the voice inside them.

Chapter Two: The Cost of Coming Home

Fort Dawn receives the party as heroes until their evidence becomes inconvenient.

Venn recognizes her cipher. She did not issue the order. Hadran d'Sivis confirms that the signature is authentic, then adds the professionally dreadful phrase “authenticity may no longer indicate authorship.” Factor Vane wants the badge and crystal sealed in the Cannith yard. Kess wants Rusk declared unstable. Nella wants the findings read aloud in the ration square.

This is the first political choice with durable weight. The party may expose everything, cooperate with a quiet inquiry, hand the evidence to a faction, or keep it. Public disclosure causes fear and several acts of foolish courage, including a citizen attempting to punch a message stone. Secrecy preserves calm while allowing the council to edit the story. Any choice creates allies and resentment. Avoid punishing openness with simple chaos. Citizens organize watches, compare strange orders, and uncover details the council missed. They also spread six false rumors and one surprisingly accurate claim that the depot is haunted by management.

That night, a message arrives from [[Redwater]]. Its purifier is producing red, metallic water. Fever has begun. The settlement requests Jorasco aid and replacement parts. The Steward recommends refusing evacuation, quarantining Redwater, and reserving medicine for Fort Dawn's “continuity population.” The phrase includes every council member and excludes most children.

Chapter Three: Redwater Arithmetic

Redwater sits around a reservoir under patchwork awnings. The purifier was built to cleanse mundane poison and low-grade magical fallout. It now hums hymns in an extinct Cyran marching cadence. Residents boil the water, which concentrates the contamination and makes the tea judgmental.

Three pressures drive the chapter:

  • Thirst: Clean reserves will last four days. Fort Dawn has enough spare water skins to evacuate only a third of the settlement.
  • Blame: A Jorasco enclave accuses the Glassborn. Local workers accuse Jorasco of creating a paid cure. Both accusations have been encouraged through forged Sivis messages.
  • Ownership: House Cannith claims the purifier's sealed core and forbids unlicensed repair. The warranty survived the nation that issued it, a triumph of civilization by some definition.

Healer Vey Sola d'Sivis, Redwater's exhausted physician, can treat the fever but refuses to rank patients by civic value. [[Bailiff Corra Vale]] keeps order with twelve volunteers and knows violence will rupture the settlement. [[Pip Marrin]], an apprentice mechanic aged fourteen, has already entered the purifier through a waste pipe twice. Every credentialed expert dismisses Pip's drawings. The drawings correctly show a second intake line.

Investigation reveals that the poison is a waste product from the purifier itself. Someone installed a regulator taken from Red Jackal gear. The device makes the purifier produce exceptionally clean water in short bursts, then dump concentrated contamination back into the reservoir. The Engine is testing whether a community will accept controlled poisoning in exchange for predictable supply.

Redwater Jobs

  • Escort medicine through a sick ward where hallucinations speak in the voices of authority figures.
  • Recover Pip after the purifier seals with the apprentice inside.
  • Negotiate water access between families, Jorasco staff, and armed workers.
  • Trace the regulator to a Red Jackal convoy moving through old military trenches.
  • Discover that Kess sold Redwater's proper replacement valve months ago to cover Fort Dawn's grain deficit.

Kess's choice saved Fort Dawn from starvation. It also made Redwater vulnerable. He will defend it with figures, and the figures are accurate. The dead remain stubbornly unimpressed.
